title: Early love of Guy Lombardo and Hal Kemp, then Count Basie's records
summary: As a boy he idolised Lombardo and Freddie Kreitzer, liked Hal Kemp's crispness, and was thrilled by Basie's first sloppy big band records and Lester's solo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: ...but when I was a kid, though, you know, before I ever heard Teddy Wilson play the piano, I was a Lombardo freak. I loved him. And I loved Carmen Lombardo singing. I loved Liebert. I loved everybody. I knew everybody's name. I was their number-one fan!
Yeah, I saw them once, when they came to my home town. And they didn't even... Not one of them got out one piece of music during the night. And they played more

tunes that night than any band I ever heard in my life, going from one to the next. I loved their piano player, Freddie Kreitzer. In fact, I even called him here. I got loaded one night here in New York, and called him in Florida. He didn't believe me at all! He says, "You mean, that Jazz piano player?" "Yup, that's me." He didn't think it was me.
What was it you liked about the band most?

I liked their sound, and I liked their... They were so crisp. That's what I liked about Hal Kemp. They were together. There was nothin' sloppy about it. And yet, when Count Basie's first records came out with his big band, they were sloppier than hell, and I just loved 'em! They were rip-roaring, whorehouse stuff, you know. Like, the very first record that he made with that big band was "Swingin' At The Daisy Chain." Well, I didn't know what a daisy chain was from... I'm from Spokane! And all of a sudden, here comes this thing. That's when I first heard Herschel, and then when Lester played that famous solo on "Time Out"... Oh, I think that's one of the greatest things I ever heard in my life.
